quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A colleague rambles for two minutes about her new mentoring program before anyone understands what it does. Say, in one sentence, what an elevator pitch is supposed to do that her two minutes didn't.
quests.correctAnswer: It tells a listener, in the time it takes to cross a lobby, what you offer and why it matters to them.
quests.hint: Think about time, clarity, and relevance together.
quests.explanation: An elevator pitch isn't a shorter speech - it's a different goal: land the point before the listener's attention moves elsewhere.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're asked to introduce your weekend project - a neighborhood tool-lending library - to someone waiting for the same bus. You have about fifteen seconds. Give the pitch.
quests.correctAnswer: We lend tools instead of everyone buying their own - drill on Tuesday, ladder on Friday, no clutter in anyone's garage.
quests.hint: Say what people get, not how the library is organized.
quests.explanation: Starting with the outcome for the listener works better than starting with how the system runs behind the scenes.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now the same bus-stop stranger mentions they just moved and don't know anyone in the building. Adjust your tool-library pitch so it also speaks to that.
quests.correctAnswer: It's how half the building has met each other - borrowing a ladder turns into knowing your neighbors.
quests.hint: Keep the same idea, but lead with the thing this particular listener just told you they want.
quests.explanation: The strongest pitch doesn't change what you offer - it changes which true thing about it you lead with.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Which sentence is clearer for a first-time listener: 'We leverage synergistic workflows to optimize cross-functional throughput,' or 'We help two teams stop waiting on each other's approvals.' Pick the clearer one and say why.
quests.correctAnswer: The second one - it names an actual problem the listener recognizes, instead of hiding behind vague business language.
quests.hint: Ask which sentence a non-expert could repeat back correctly.
quests.explanation: Clarity means a stranger could immediately explain it back to someone else. Buzzwords fail that test even when they sound impressive.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Rewrite this into plain, clear language a twelve-year-old could follow: 'Our platform facilitates the seamless aggregation of disparate scheduling data to drive operational efficiencies.'
quests.correctAnswer: It pulls everyone's schedules into one place, so nobody has to chase people down to find a meeting time.
quests.hint: Ask what the software actually does for a real person, in everyday words.
quests.explanation: Translating jargon into a concrete action - 'pulls schedules into one place' - is what makes a technical idea land instantly.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A teammate wants to pitch their new internal wiki tool to the whole office and asks for one clear sentence they can say out loud tomorrow. Give them one.
quests.correctAnswer: Instead of five people answering the same question five times, the answer lives in one place everyone can find.
quests.hint: Picture someone actually saying it out loud in a hallway - does it still make sense?
quests.explanation: A pitch built to be spoken, not read, uses shorter clauses and a rhythm that matches normal conversation.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Before pitching your idea for a shared office plant-watering schedule, what's the first question a smart pitcher asks themselves?
quests.correctAnswer: What does this specific listener actually care about right now?
quests.hint: Think about what comes before choosing any words at all.
quests.explanation: Every other pitching skill sits on top of this one - you can't choose the right words until you know who you're choosing them for.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're pitching a carpool app. One listener is a parent worried about safety. Another is a student worried about cost. Give the version for the parent.
quests.correctAnswer: Every driver is verified and every ride is tracked in real time, so you always know exactly who your child is riding with.
quests.hint: Lead with the worry this listener actually has, not the app's full feature list.
quests.explanation: The parent doesn't need to hear about cost savings first - naming their actual concern earns their attention before anything else does.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Same carpool app, now pitch it to the cost-conscious student instead - without repeating the safety-focused version word for word.
quests.correctAnswer: Split a ten-mile commute four ways and gas money stops being a monthly headache.
quests.hint: Swap the lead concern, not just a few adjectives - the whole opening should feel different.
quests.explanation: Adapting a pitch means rebuilding the opening around a different concern, not just substituting a word here and there.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Which of these pitch openings actually names a real problem: 'Our app has twelve features and a sleek design,' or 'Most people forget to take medication at the right time.' Choose and explain briefly.
quests.correctAnswer: The second one - it names a specific, relatable frustration before ever mentioning a solution.
quests.hint: A feature list isn't a problem. Ask which sentence a listener would nod along to.
quests.explanation: Listing features assumes interest that hasn't been earned yet. Naming a real problem earns it first.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch jumps straight to the solution with no problem stated: 'Our app sends you a reminder chime at exactly the right time.' Add one sentence before it that gives the pitch a problem to solve.
quests.correctAnswer: It's easy to lose track of a pill schedule in a busy day, and missing a dose matters more than most errands do. Our app sends you a reminder chime at exactly the right time.
quests.hint: Name the everyday moment where the problem actually shows up.
quests.explanation: Grounding the problem in a specific moment - 'a busy day' - makes it feel real instead of generic.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now do the same thing for a different idea: a laundromat app that tells you which machines are free before you walk over. Write a problem-first opening.
quests.correctAnswer: Nobody wants to lug a basket two blocks just to find every machine taken. Our app shows you which ones are free before you leave your apartment.
quests.hint: Picture the specific annoying moment, then work backward to the app.
quests.explanation: The same structure - name the annoyance, then the fix - works across completely different ideas once you've learned it.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch says: 'Renters often don't know their legal rights. We built a chatbot.' What's missing between those two sentences?
quests.correctAnswer: The connective tissue - how exactly the chatbot addresses not knowing your rights is never explained; the two sentences just sit side by side.
quests.hint: Ask whether the solution sentence actually answers the problem sentence.
quests.explanation: A problem and a solution stated back to back isn't the same as connecting them - the listener needs the bridge spelled out.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Fix that renters'-rights pitch so the problem and solution are actually connected in one flowing sentence.
quests.correctAnswer: When your landlord ignores a repair request, you can ask our chatbot what your local law actually requires and get a straight answer in seconds.
quests.hint: Use the solution to directly resolve the exact problem you named, in the same breath.
quests.explanation: Connecting problem to solution means the second half of the sentence directly resolves the tension the first half created.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Apply the same connecting technique to a new idea: an app that finds the cheapest time to book a flight. Write one connected sentence, not two separate ones.
quests.correctAnswer: Prices for the same flight can swing by hundreds of dollars in a week, so our app tells you the exact day to book instead of you guessing.
quests.hint: Write it as a single sentence where the second half directly answers the first.
quests.explanation: One flowing sentence, rather than a problem statement followed by a solution statement, is what makes a pitch feel effortless to listen to.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: 'This backpack has a padded laptop sleeve' is a feature. Turn it into a benefit for a commuting student.
quests.correctAnswer: Your laptop survives the crush of a packed train, even on the days you can't get a seat.
quests.hint: A feature is what it has. A benefit is what changes for the person.
quests.explanation: The feature stays the same fact - the benefit translates that fact into something the listener actually experiences.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Here's a weak pitch that only lists features: 'It has a padded sleeve, a water-resistant zip, and a hidden pocket.' Rewrite it around the one benefit that matters most for a commuter.
quests.correctAnswer: Rain or a crowded platform, your laptop and your valuables stay exactly where you left them.
quests.hint: Pick one benefit and build the whole sentence around it, instead of listing every feature.
quests.explanation: Cramming in every feature dilutes the pitch. One well-chosen benefit is more memorable than three unconnected facts.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Take a different feature - 'this water bottle keeps drinks cold for twenty-four hours' - and pitch it as a benefit to someone training for a summer marathon.
quests.correctAnswer: Fill it before sunrise, and it's still ice-cold at your last mile in the afternoon heat.
quests.hint: Connect the feature to a moment specific to marathon training, not cold drinks in general.
quests.explanation: Tying a benefit to a specific, vivid moment in the listener's life makes it land far harder than a general claim.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Spot the jargon in this pitch and name it: 'We disrupt the legacy paradigm of onboarding through a frictionless, best-in-class solution.'
quests.correctAnswer: Nearly every phrase is jargon - 'disrupt,' 'legacy paradigm,' 'frictionless,' and 'best-in-class' - none of it says what the product actually does.
quests.hint: Ask which words could be deleted without losing any actual information.
quests.explanation: A useful test for jargon: if removing the word changes nothing about what the listener understands, it wasn't doing any work.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now rewrite that onboarding pitch in plain language, keeping it to one sentence.
quests.correctAnswer: New hires get their laptop, logins, and first task ready before they even sit down on day one.
quests.hint: Describe an actual moment on someone's first day.
quests.explanation: Plain language survives being said out loud in a real conversation - jargon usually doesn't.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A friend pitching their consulting business says: 'I optimize synergies to unlock scalable value for stakeholders.' Help them say what they actually do, in one plain sentence.
quests.correctAnswer: I find the one process that's quietly wasting your team the most time, and fix it.
quests.hint: Ask them directly: what do you actually do for a client, in a sentence a client would use themselves?
quests.explanation: If your own client wouldn't use those words to describe you, the pitch is speaking to itself, not to the listener.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This sentence has filler dragging it down: 'So basically, what we're kind of trying to do here is sort of help people save a little time.' Cut it to one clean sentence.
quests.correctAnswer: We help people save time.
quests.hint: Remove every word that could disappear without losing meaning.
quests.explanation: Filler words don't add nuance - they add hesitation. Removing them makes a pitch sound more confident, not less careful.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Trim this pitch without losing any real information: 'Our app, which we've been working on for a while now, is basically a tool that kind of helps you remember to drink more water throughout your day.'
quests.correctAnswer: Our app reminds you to drink water throughout the day.
quests.hint: Ask what's left if you delete every hedge word and every mention of how long you worked on it.
quests.explanation: Cutting filler isn't about sounding curt - it's about respecting the fifteen seconds you actually have.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Take this rambling introduction of yourself and compress it to two clean sentences: 'Hi, so, um, I'm someone who's been in marketing for a while, and I guess what I really enjoy is kind of figuring out what makes people click on things, if that makes sense.'
quests.correctAnswer: I'm a marketer. I figure out exactly what makes people click, and why.
quests.hint: Find the actual claim buried in the sentence, then say only that.
quests.explanation: Two short, confident sentences carry more authority than one long, hedging one - even when the information is identical.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A founder starts her pitch with: 'So this idea actually came to me three years ago when I was living in Chicago and working a totally different job...' Is that detail worth keeping in an elevator pitch? Why or why not?
quests.correctAnswer: No - the origin story doesn't tell the listener what the product does or why it matters to them right now.
quests.hint: Ask whether the detail changes what the listener understands about the product itself.
quests.explanation: Backstory can be compelling in a longer conversation, but in fifteen seconds it spends time the actual pitch needs.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Cut the unnecessary detail from this pitch and keep only what the listener needs: 'We built this in six months with a team of four, working out of a co-working space downtown, and it's an app that helps freelancers track unpaid invoices.'
quests.correctAnswer: It's an app that helps freelancers track unpaid invoices.
quests.hint: Keep the sentence that says what it does. Cut everything about how or where it was built.
quests.explanation: A listener in an elevator doesn't need your production history - they need to know what changes for them.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now do it yourself: you're pitching a community garden plot-sharing app. Write a pitch that includes zero backstory and zero technical detail - just what changes for the listener.
quests.correctAnswer: Instead of a waitlist for garden plots, you share one with three neighbors and everyone gets fresh vegetables without owning the whole bed.
quests.hint: Picture the listener as someone who wants a garden plot, not someone who wants to hear how the app was made.
quests.explanation: Leaving out every detail that doesn't serve the listener is a discipline, not a shortcut - it takes more editing, not less.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch tries to say four things at once: 'Our app tracks your sleep, your steps, your water intake, and connects with your calendar.' What's the core problem with trying to say all four in one pitch?
quests.correctAnswer: None of them get enough room to actually land - the listener leaves remembering nothing specific instead of one clear thing.
quests.hint: Ask what a listener would repeat back five minutes later.
quests.explanation: A pitch that tries to cover everything usually ends up memorable for nothing. One clear message beats four vague ones.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: From that same four-feature app, pick the single strongest message and build one clean pitch around just that.
quests.correctAnswer: One glance in the morning tells you if last night's sleep was actually enough to power through today.
quests.hint: Choose whichever benefit is most immediately useful to a listener, and drop the rest for this pitch.
quests.explanation: Choosing one message doesn't mean the other features don't exist - it means this particular fifteen seconds isn't trying to sell all of them.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're at a job fair with thirty seconds to introduce yourself to a recruiter. You've done marketing, some design work, and ran a small side business. Pick one main message and pitch yourself.
quests.correctAnswer: I turn half-finished ideas into things people actually buy - I've done it for my own small business and I want to do it at scale for you.
quests.hint: Resist listing everything you've done. Choose the one thread a recruiter would remember.
quests.explanation: The same discipline that shapes a product pitch shapes a personal one: one clear thread beats a full résumé read aloud.
